column3: The Big Five, by the end of middle school

column4: Understand that, according to the U.S. Constitution, treaties are "the supreme law of the land"; consequently treaty rights supersede most state laws.
column5: Understanding why treaty rights outrank state law
column12: Exemplary — You explain why treaties outrank most state laws, and use a court case to show what that means today.
column14: Proficient — You explain that treaties are the supreme law of the land, so treaty rights come before most state laws.
column16: Progressing — You say treaties are important without explaining where their power comes from.
column18: Beginning — You can name treaty rights without knowing what backs them yet.

column4: Understand that Tribal sovereignty has cultural, political, and economic bases.
column5: Explaining what tribal sovereignty rests on
column12: Exemplary — You explain the cultural, political, and economic sides of sovereignty, and how they hold each other up.
column14: Proficient — You explain that tribal sovereignty has cultural, political, and economic bases, with an example of each.
column16: Progressing — You define sovereignty but explain only one of the things it rests on.
column18: Beginning — You can use the word sovereignty without explaining what it rests on yet.

column4: Understand that Tribes are subject to federal law and taxes, as well as some state regulations.
column5: Explaining which laws reach tribal nations
column12: Exemplary — You explain which laws reach tribal nations and which do not, and use an example to show where the line falls.
column14: Proficient — You explain that tribal nations are subject to federal law and taxes, and to some state regulations.
column16: Progressing — You say tribal nations have their own laws without explaining what else applies.
column18: Beginning — You can name tribal governments without knowing which laws reach them yet.

column4: Understand that Tribal sovereignty is ever-evolving and therefore levels of sovereignty and status vary from Tribe to Tribe.
column5: Recognizing that sovereignty differs from nation to nation
column12: Exemplary — You explain how sovereignty differs between tribal nations, and what has changed it over time.
column14: Proficient — You explain that tribal sovereignty keeps changing, and that its level varies from nation to nation.
column16: Progressing — You treat all tribal nations as having the same status.
column18: Beginning — You can name tribal nations without comparing their status yet.

column4: Understand that there were and are frequent and continued threats to Tribal sovereignty that are mostly addressed through the courts.
column5: Tracing how tribal nations defend sovereignty in court
column12: Exemplary — You trace a threat to sovereignty through the courts, and explain what the ruling changed.
column14: Proficient — You explain that threats to tribal sovereignty continue, and that they are mostly answered in court.
column16: Progressing — You name a threat to sovereignty without explaining how it was answered.
column18: Beginning — You can say sovereignty is challenged without examples yet.

column4: How does the physical geography affect Northwest Tribes' culture, economy, and where they choose to settle and trade?
column5: Investigating how geography shapes Northwest tribal life
column12: Exemplary — You explain how geography shaped culture, economy, and trade together for a specific tribal nation.
column14: Proficient — You explain how the physical geography of a place shaped a tribal nation's culture, economy, and trade.
column16: Progressing — You describe the land or the culture, but you don't connect them.
column18: Beginning — You can locate tribal homelands without explaining what the land made possible yet.

column4: What is the legal status of the Tribes who negotiated or who did not enter into United States treaties?
column5: Comparing the legal status of tribal nations
column12: Exemplary — You compare the status of nations that entered treaties and those that did not, and explain what follows from each.
column14: Proficient — You explain how a tribal nation’s legal status depends on whether it entered a treaty with the United States.
column16: Progressing — You say some nations signed treaties without explaining what that changed.
column18: Beginning — You can name treaties without connecting them to legal status yet.

column4: What were the political, economic, and cultural forces that led to the treaties?
column12: Exemplary — You explain the political, economic, and cultural pressures behind a treaty, and which pressed hardest.
column14: Proficient — You explain the political, economic, and cultural forces that led to a treaty.
column16: Progressing — You name one reason for a treaty without the others.
column18: Beginning — You can say treaties happened without explaining why yet.

column4: What are the ways in which Tribes respond to the threats and outside pressure to extinguish their cultures and independence?
column5: Explaining how tribal nations protect their ways of life
column12: Exemplary — You explain several ways a nation protected its culture and independence, and what each one cost or won.
column14: Proficient — You explain ways tribal nations have responded to pressure to give up their cultures and independence.
column16: Progressing — You name a threat without explaining how the nation responded.
column18: Beginning — You can say cultures were threatened without examples of how nations answered yet.

column4: What do local Tribes do to meet the challenges of reservation life; and, as sovereign nations, to meet the economic and cultural needs of their Tribal communities?
column5: Explaining how tribal nations meet their communities’ needs today
column12: Exemplary — You explain how a nation meets economic and cultural needs today, and connect that work to its sovereignty.
column14: Proficient — You explain what a tribal nation does today to meet the economic and cultural needs of its community.
column16: Progressing — You describe reservation life without what the nation is doing about it.
column18: Beginning — You can name a reservation without knowing what its government does yet.
